chunks: From him, from al-Qasim, from 'Ali, from Abi Basir, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:
“For a tooth, there are five camels; its farthest and nearest are equal. And for a finger, there are ten camels.”

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The correct way regarding these two reports, and regarding the narration of al-Halabi and 'Abd Allah ibn Sinan mentioned earlier, is that we interpret the fingers intended by them as excluding the thumb, for the thumb has an independent ruling, as we shall mention later. And regarding the narration of Zarif ibn Nasih and what it contains of the ruling of the teeth, the correct way in it as well is what we mentioned before: that the front teeth are equal in the ruling of blood money, and the back teeth are also equal, even if there is a difference between the front teeth and the back teeth, as we have explained.

key_terms.الدِّيَةِ: blood money; legally prescribed financial compensation for injury
key_terms.السِّنِّ: a tooth, in the context of prescribed blood money compensation
key_terms.الْأَسْنَانِ: the teeth, discussed collectively in relation to compensation rulings
key_terms.الْإِبِلِ: camels, the unit in which diyah is quantified here
key_terms.الْإِبْهَامَ: the thumb, treated as having a separate legal ruling
key_terms.الْإِصْبَعِ: a finger, for which a specific diyah amount is stated
key_terms.الْمَقَادِيمَ: the front teeth, equal among themselves in the diyah ruling
key_terms.الْمَوَاخِيرُ: the back teeth, equal among themselves in the diyah ruling

ai.seo_question: What is the diyah for a tooth or a finger in Shia hadith, and how are differing reports reconciled?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the diyah for injury to teeth and fingers. The compiler explains how apparently differing reports are reconciled: the ruling on fingers excludes the thumb, which has a separate ruling, and the teeth are grouped so that front teeth are equal among themselves and back teeth are equal among themselves in diyah.
